title: Interior materials and electronics
audience: Car detailers working on vehicle interiors, trim, screens and electronic controls.
learningOutcomes: Identify interior materials and match the cleaning method to each.
Keep liquid away from electronic controls, screens and airbag areas.
Stop and record a warning light, a fault or exposed wiring.

instruction.heading: Identify the material before you choose a product
instruction.body: Most vehicle interiors combine several materials, and each one reacts differently to a cleaner or a dressing. Fabric seats and carpet hold dirt in the fibres. Leather, vinyl and rubber can dry, crack or go tacky when the wrong product sits on them. Plastic trim can mark under a harsh solvent. Many surfaces described as leather are coated or synthetic, sometimes sold as leatherette, so check each surface by look and touch and by the owner's information rather than assuming. Where the surface is unclear, choose the mildest product the label allows and test it first. Record the material you decided on before the product goes on. The order of an interior clean and the protection step are covered in “Interior cleaning and treatment” (interior cleaning and treatment). This lesson covers the material, electronics and fault checks that come first, so read it alongside that lesson rather than in place of it.

instruction.heading: Choosing a product and testing it
instruction.body: The label and the safety data sheet decide what a product may be used on. The guides this lesson is drawn from show dressings that can be diluted to give anything from a natural finish to a high gloss, and very glossy results on leather or trim are seldom what an owner wants. For this lesson, a natural, non-greasy finish is the default on leather and trim, unless the owner's written instruction and the product label both allow something else. Dilute only as the label directs, and label every spray bottle with the product, the dilution and the date. Test on a hidden area first, such as under the edge of a seat or inside a door pocket, and let the test area dry fully before you judge it. A test that dries tacky, cloudy or discoloured means the product is wrong for that surface, so stop and choose another. Do not use heat to speed up a product. The Auto-Detailing guide describes using a hair dryer or heated seats to make leather more receptive to a product. Heat inside a closed cabin needs its own risk assessment, so this lesson does not adopt that method.

instruction.heading: Screens, controls and sensors
instruction.body: Screens, instrument displays, switches, dash buttons, steering wheel controls and seat sensors are electronic, so keep liquid off them. Do not spray any product onto these components. Put the product onto an applicator or cloth first, wipe the surface with that, and use a dry microfibre cloth alone for dust. The Spanish-language manual warns against spraying dressing directly onto plastic because it can leave marks, and the same reasoning applies to a display. Screen coatings vary, and the manufacturer's care guidance governs where it is available. Where no guidance can be found, use a dry or lightly dampened cloth and stop if the surface does not respond. Keep the cloths used on screens separate from those used on leather and trim, so residue from a trim product is not carried onto a display. This separation is working practice, not a regulatory requirement.

instruction.heading: Airbags, wiring and warning lights
instruction.body: Airbag covers, the steering column area, side airbag modules and any exposed wiring are outside detailing work. Do not remove, pry or press on a cover, do not clean inside a gap around a module, and do not disturb a loose wire. If you find a loose cover or an exposed wire, stop work on that part, photograph it, record its location, and tell the customer in writing that a qualified repairer should inspect it. If a warning light or fault message is showing when the vehicle arrives, or appears during the work, record it as found. Do not reset it, clear it or try to diagnose it. Electrical and airbag diagnosis and repair are not part of detailing, and completing this lesson does not qualify anyone to carry out that work.

instruction.heading: Cabin conditions and handover
instruction.body: Plan the handover around dryness. Keep carpets and seats as dry as you can, because damp material holds moisture against the floor and cushioning for longer than the owner expects. Check seats, mats and the floor for damp patches before handover. Record anything still wet, and tell the owner how to dry it. Protectants go on only to dry surfaces, as “Interior cleaning and treatment” describes. Ventilate the cabin when the label or safety data sheet calls for it. Read “Cabin air and vapour exposure” (cabin air and vapour exposure) before any solvent-containing product is used in a closed cabin, because vapour in a hot, closed vehicle is a separate risk with its own controls. A written record of what you found, with the time and location, protects the owner and the business if a later question arises about a surface or a component.

procedure: Identify each interior material and note it on the job sheet before you choose a product.
Read the label and the safety data sheet for the product, then test it on a hidden area.
Dilute only as the label directs, and label the spray bottle with the product, dilution and date.
Apply product to an applicator or cloth first, and keep liquid off screens, controls, sensors and airbag areas.
If a warning light, fault message, loose airbag cover or exposed wire is found, stop work on that part, photograph it and record it as found.
Tell the customer in writing what was found, and recommend a qualified repairer where the item needs one.
Protect only dry surfaces that the label names, and wipe off the excess.
Check for damp areas before handover, and record the result.

workedExamples.situation: A customer asks you to spray a cleaner straight onto the dash display and the climate controls, because the display is smeared.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you do with the display and the controls, and what do you tell the customer?
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not spray liquid onto the display or the controls. Dampen a microfibre cloth with a product the label allows, or use a dry cloth alone, and wipe the display gently. Explain that spray can enter electronic components and leave marks. If the smear will not come off with a cloth, record its condition and do not use a stronger product to remove it.

workedExamples.situation: A coated leather seat and a vinyl door card are both dirty. The owner wants a high-gloss finish to match the dashboard.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Which surfaces need a test, and what finish do you aim for?
workedExamples.reasoning: Identify both surfaces and record them. Test the cleaner on a hidden area of the seat and on the inside of the door card, and let each test dry. Aim for a natural, non-greasy finish on both. Record the owner's request for a gloss finish. Do not apply a glossy product to the leather unless the owner gives written instruction and the product label allows it. Confirm the agreed finish in the job record.

workedExamples.situation: During a cabin clean, a warning light appears on the instrument cluster. The owner says it was on before the car came in.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you record, and what do you do with the cluster?
workedExamples.reasoning: Photograph the cluster with the light showing, and note the time and the owner's statement as found. Leave the cluster alone. Do not reset the light, clear a code or diagnose the cause. Tell the owner in writing that the light needs inspection by a qualified repairer, and record that the referral was made. Continue on other areas that do not involve the affected system.

workedExamples.situation: While wiping the steering wheel trim, you notice a loose cover near the airbag area and a wire showing beneath it.
workedExamples.reasoning: Stop work on that area, and do not touch the cover or the wire. Photograph the item and record its location. Tell the customer that a qualified repairer should inspect it, and note the referral on the job sheet. Do not treat the item as a detailing task.

equipmentAndPpe: Labelled applicators for each material, and microfibre cloths kept in separate groups for screens, leather and trim.
Soft brushes for vents and seams, and a torch for checking damp areas.
Labelled spray bottles for diluted products, with the dilution and date recorded.
Camera or phone for photographing each finding before any work starts on that item.

PPE: gloves and eye protection where the product's safety data sheet names them. Ventilation where the label or safety data sheet calls for it. Respiratory protection only where the safety data sheet and a risk assessment require it, because PPE is the last control in the hierarchy.

commonErrors.error: Spraying product onto a screen, dash display or control.
commonErrors.prevention: Apply product to an applicator or cloth first, and keep liquid off the component.

commonErrors.error: Treating a coated or synthetic leather surface as raw leather.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the surface, follow the label, and test on a hidden area first.

commonErrors.error: Choosing a high-gloss finish for leather or trim.
commonErrors.prevention: Default to a natural, non-greasy finish unless the owner's written instruction and the label both allow otherwise.

commonErrors.error: Using heat to speed up a product inside a closed cabin.
commonErrors.prevention: Do not use heat as a shortcut. Wait for the label's dwell time, and do not use a method that needs its own risk assessment.

commonErrors.error: Resetting a warning light, or pressing on an airbag cover to see whether it is loose.
commonErrors.prevention: Record the item as found, stop work on it, and refer it to a qualified repairer.

commonErrors.error: Handing over seats or carpet that are still damp.
commonErrors.prevention: Check for damp patches before handover, record any that remain, and tell the owner how to dry them.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Victorian WorkSafe guidance says a business must keep a register of the hazardous substances at its workplace, and that supplied containers should carry the Australian manufacturer or importer's details (WorkSafe Victoria, Hazardous substances: safety basics; page reviewed 30/07/2022). Safe Work Australia says safety data sheets must be easy to reach for workers who use, handle or store the product (Safe Work Australia, Using safety data sheets; no page date shown). Check that each product for the job has a safety data sheet and a label that names its supplier before use. Other states and territories apply their own WHS authorities and rules, so confirm the position where you work.

Control hierarchy: remove or replace the hazard first, then isolate it or use engineering controls such as extraction, then administrative controls, with PPE as the last control (WorkSafe Victoria, Hazardous substances: safety basics). Where a product or task leaves a risk in place, record the controls used.

Safe Work Australia's model WHS guidance treats an exposure to a hazardous chemical that needs treatment within 48 hours as a notifiable incident, which must be reported to the regulator quickly (Safe Work Australia, WHS duties related to hazardous chemicals; no page date shown). If a worker or customer is affected by a product used on a job, stop the task, arrange treatment and follow the business's incident procedure.

Airbag and supplementary restraint system components, and electrical systems in the vehicle, are not detailing work. This lesson does not grant any automotive, electrical or airbag licence or authority.
Cabin vapour and ventilation for solvent-containing products are covered in “Cabin air and vapour exposure” (cabin air and vapour exposure). This lesson does not repeat that content.

qualityStandard: Each interior material is identified and recorded before a product is chosen.
Each product is used only on a surface its label lists, and no glossy or greasy finish is applied to leather or trim without written instruction and label support.
No liquid reaches screens, controls, sensors or airbag areas, and no panel covering an airbag or wiring is disturbed.
Any warning light, fault, loose cover or exposed wire is recorded, photographed and reported to the customer, and the interior is dry at handover with any damp area recorded.
documentationEvidence: Material identification for each interior surface, with the product and the label or safety data sheet reference used.
Test-area record for each product: location, product, dwell time and result.
Photographs and written record of any warning light, fault, loose cover or exposed wire, with the time, location and the customer informed.
Handover dryness check, with any damp area recorded and the owner's drying instruction.
summary: Identify each material before you choose a product, and test on a hidden area first.
Keep liquid away from screens, controls, sensors and airbag areas, and apply product to a cloth first.
Default to a natural, non-greasy finish on leather and trim, and do not use heat as a shortcut.
Record and refer any warning light, fault, loose cover or exposed wire. Do not reset or repair it.

knowledgeChecks.question: Before you choose a product for a vehicle interior surface, what should you do first?
options: Pick the strongest product you have on hand for the job today
Spray a test onto the middle of the seat, where the stain shows most clearly
Identify the material and check the label or safety data sheet for it

knowledgeChecks.question: A dash display is smeared. Which method is correct?
options: Put product on a cloth, wipe gently, and keep liquid off the display
Spray the cleaner onto the display and wipe it with a dry cloth
Soak a towel and press it onto the display to lift the smear
Use a dressing straight from the bottle onto the display face

knowledgeChecks.question: During a cabin clean you see a warning light on the instrument cluster. What is the correct action?
options: Reset the light so the owner is not worried about it at pickup today
Stop work on that system, record the light as found, and tell the customer
Clear the fault code with a scanner, so the light goes off for the owner

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the correct condition of a vehicle interior at handover?
options: Seats still damp, to be dried by the owner later
Protected while still wet, to seal in the moisture
Dry, with any damp area checked and recorded
